query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, dense anti‐oxidation surface coating (e.g. an alumina‐based or silicide coating) to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will significantly improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures without compromising its inherent mechanical performance at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with a single-phase (BCC) structure, exhibiting 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but showing inadequate oxygen resistance (pesting) during high‐temperature air exposure.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin, adherent oxidation-resistant coating (for example, via chemical vapor deposition, physical vapor deposition, or electrospark deposition) that forms a protective alumina or silicide scale on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure in air at temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C for durations around 5 hours under strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, conditions mimicking service environments where the alloy would be mechanically loaded.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, dense, and adherent oxide (or silicide) scale at the surface interface, which acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen.
generation.mechanism: The coating reduces the oxygen uptake by impeding diffusion into the substrate, thereby preventing pesting and oxidation-induced degradation while preserving the microstructural integrity that governs the alloy’s high strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will exhibit a marked reduction in oxidation (lower mass gain and less pronounced oxide scale formation) and maintain its tensile properties (ductility and yield strength) at both room and high temperatures compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr deteriorates through rapid oxidation when exposed to elevated temperatures in air, which undermines its mechanical performance despite its attractive strength and ductility characteristics.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective for high-temperature applications (up to ~1000 °C) in air and under similar strain rates and exposure durations. The coating must be thin enough to avoid altering the bulk mechanical response, and the process parameters should be optimized to ensure coating adherence and compatibility with the substrate.
generation.uncertainty: Exact coating composition, optimal thickness, and deposition conditions require further optimization. Additionally, potential interactions at the coating–substrate interface could affect local mechanical behavior if not properly controlled.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identically fabricated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples. Apply the proposed thin anti-oxidation coating to one set using a controlled deposition method (e.g., alumina coating via PVD), while leaving the other set uncoated. Subject both sets to air exposure at 800–1000 °C for 5 hours under controlled strain rates (10−4–10−2 s−1) that simulate service conditions.
measurements: Quantitative mass gain measurements to track oxidation rate
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analyses (SEM, XRD) to assess coating integrity and oxide scale formation
Tensile tests (yield strength, ductility) before and after exposure
Adhesion and interfacial integrity tests of the coating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples exhibit no significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., similar mass gain and oxide scale characteristics as the uncoated samples) or if their post-exposure mechanical properties (tensile strength and ductility) degrade relative to those of the uncoated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect
